newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN delays entry of strife-torn Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN delays entry of strife-torn Cambodia.

text.p: The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Thursday decided to postpone Cambodia's entry into the group but will still admit Burma and Laos later this month, sources in the grouping said.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi was expected to make an announcement on the matter at a news conference scheduled for 4:30 p.m. (0830 GMT) on Thursday.
ASEAN, whose foreign ministers were holding an emergency meeting in the Malaysian capital, had been planning to admit Cambodia along with Burma and Laos at its annual meeting this month.
But Cambodian Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's power grab over the weekend threw that plan into disarray.
At least 58 people have died and up to 200 have been wounded in clashes between forces loyal to Hun Sen and those of his rival, First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh.

A statement to be issued on Thursday would reiterate ASEAN's policy of not interfering in neighbouring countries' affairs. It would also state the importance of stability in Cambodia to the region, the sources said.

But the grouping has a long history of diplomatic involvement in Cambodia. Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas was an architect of the accords that Washington said on Tuesday had been ruptured by Hun Sen.
In Phnom Penh, Hun Sen told reporters before the decision was announced that Cambodia's troubles were "our internal business".
"ASEAN countries must let us solve our problems on our own," he said. "Please stay out of our internal business."
Malaysia is this year's chairman of ASEAN, which also includes Indonesia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
ASEAN heads of state decided at an informal summit in Jakarta last year to admit its final three members as a group, and left it to their foreign ministers to fix the induction date.
The foreign ministers on May 31 decided to admit the three during the grouping's annual meeting to be held on July 21-29 in the Malaysian capital.

The decision was heavily criticised by Western governments and human rights groups that want to isolate Burma over its human rights record and its crackdown on a democracy movement led by Aung San Suu Kyi.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington had "given some advice" to ASEAN for its Thursday meeting. He refused to say specifically what that advice was.

"It's very important at a time like this when there's chaos in Cambodia, when they're on the verge of a civil war, when fighting is occurring throughout the country between forces of the two major political parties, for countries that have an interest in Cambodia to speak out about what is acceptable and what is not acceptable," he said.
